title: A world in a grain of sand
hook: Blake: see a world in a grain of sand

segments.voice: Yesterday, Wordsworth's presence, living in sunsets and sky and the mind that sees them. Your line was a joy strong enough to unsettle. Today the awe shrinks down to something you could lose under a fingernail.

Pour a little salt onto a dark table. Each grain is tiny and rough-edged, easy never to give a second look. The last few days have been about big things: infinite spaces, the starry heavens, the round ocean. Today a poet points the other way. William Blake begins a poem not with the sky but with the smallest thing on a beach, and says the whole world is in it. Not a picture of the world. The world.
screen: `A LITTLE SALT ON A DARK TABLE.` → `FROM THE STARS TO A GRAIN.` → `THE WORLD IS IN IT.`

segments.voice: Here are the opening lines of Blake's Auguries of Innocence: "To see a World in a Grain of Sand and a Heaven in a Wild Flower, Hold Infinity in the palm of your hand and Eternity in an hour." Four pairs, each small beside large. First, a world in a grain. Notice the verb: to see. Blake isn't making a claim about sand. He's describing a way of looking, close enough and long enough that the small thing opens. Second, a heaven in a wild flower. Not a garden rose: a wild one, the kind nobody planted and nobody waters. Third, infinity in your hand, eternity in an hour. The biggest things there are, set inside a palm and a single hour. Some readers hear a promise that the ordinary day is big enough. Fourth, the part that's easy to miss: the poem keeps going, in a long run of couplets, and many aren't about beauty at all. They're about harm, to caged birds, starved dogs, hunted hares, and to people too. The very first: "A Robin Red breast in a Cage puts all Heaven in a Rage." The same seeing that finds heaven in a flower finds heaven's anger at a caged bird. If a grain holds a world, a small cruelty isn't small either. The tiny thing is holy, and so the tiny wrong matters.
screen: `A WORLD IN A GRAIN` · `A HEAVEN IN A WILD FLOWER` · `INFINITY IN YOUR HAND` · `SMALL THINGS MATTER BOTH WAYS` · then, large: `A WORLD IN A GRAIN.`

segments.voice: Put one small thing on your palm or on something dark: a grain of rice, salt or sand, a seed, a crumb of soil. Look only at it, its edges, its color, whether it catches light, and when the mind wanders, bring it back to the grain. You don't have to see a world; just keep looking, and see what the looking does.
Blake. The poet whose way of seeing holds a world in a grain of sand, a heaven in a wild flower, and finds that small harms matter too. Today's word.
Your line: a world in a grain. Blake's way of seeing cuts both ways. That's day one thousand nineteen.

howItsDone: Some people on a personal spiritual path practice close looking at one small object, a seed, a stone, a grain, as a short daily meditation, and Blake's opening lines are often read alongside it.

chat.says: What did Blake mean by seeing 'a world in a grain of sand'?
options: A way of looking so closely that small things open, and small harms matter too.
That every grain of sand is a tiny planet, in a literal scientific sense.
That small things are pretty, so we should collect them from beaches.
chat.meaning: Blake describes a way of seeing: look long enough and the small thing opens. His couplets then show small cruelties matter too, like a caged robin.

notes: Quotations run the lines together; editions differ in capitals and punctuation, and some print 'Robin Redbreast' as one word. Confirm against the Pickering manuscript or a standard edition.
'One of the first' couplets: the robin couplet follows the opening quatrain directly in standard editions; confirm.
'four pairs' counts the four small/large pairs in the opening quatrain, which the quoted text shows directly.
'this part rarely makes the greeting cards' is a light aside, not a claim about publishing; cut if a reviewer prefers.

Editor pass: cut the unsourced aside about greeting cards; 'one of the first' couplets made 'the very first', since the robin couplet directly follows the opening quatrain.

Audit pass: the couplets were described as all 'about harm to small creatures'; the poem also turns to human suffering and injustice (the beggar, the harlot, the soldier), so the teach now says many are about harm, to animals and to people.
